name: list-steps

capacity.note: past five steps the row crowds and a split paces one step per page; a split run paces ONE step per page and carries a derived “→ next: …” signal (§0b connected members)

density.note: one sentence per step, not a paragraph. The strip gives every card the tallest card's height, so one long step tightens the whole row, and a body that outgrows the card spills past its bottom edge and is clipped at the stage

description: Horizontal row of ordered step cards, each with a full description body (the `vertical` variant stacks them instead).
purpose: Use for richer sequential processes where each step needs a paragraph rather than a label. More verbose than timeline; more structured than a plain ordered list.

steps.description: Ordered list; each li gets a step number. Body can be one paragraph or a nested bullet list.

skeleton:
<!-- _class: list-steps -->

## How to roll this out.

1. First step — a sentence describing what you do here.
2. Second step — a sentence describing what you do here.
3. Third step — a sentence describing what you do here.
4. Fourth step — a sentence describing what you do here.
sample:
<!-- _class: list-steps -->

## Steps promise an order and keep it.

1. Name the step
   - A verb-first title and one clause of body.
2. Keep steps parallel
   - Same shape every step, or sequence breaks.
3. Number honestly
   - Order is the promise this layout makes.
4. Stop at five
   - Six fits; seven is two slides.

stressDoc.summary: Six steps — the last honest sequence.
stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: list-steps -->

## Five steps is the last honest sequence.

1. Open at full strength
   - A step carries a verb, an object, and one condition.
2. Hold the parallel line
   - Six survive only if every body stays one clause.
3. Front-load the risk
   - The contested step goes up top.
4. Shorten as you descend
   - The reader is walking, not studying.
5. Stop
   - A sixth step is a second slide.

whenToUse.title: Steps need a sentence each
whenToUse.body: When each step carries a label plus a sentence of description. Lighter rosters of steps with short labels use the `timeline` variant; richer descriptions belong on the default cards.

whenToUse.title: Three to five steps
whenToUse.body: Two steps wastes the layout's ledger feel; six begins to crowd. Group adjacent steps or split the process at a natural phase break.

whenToUse.title: Prefix word names the unit
whenToUse.body: The default `STEP` prefix can swap to `PHASE`, `STAGE`, `MILESTONE`, `RANK`, or `TIER`. Pick the noun that matches how the audience already thinks about the process.

antiPatterns.title: Light labels, no body
antiPatterns.body: If each step is a single label with no description, use the `timeline` variant (dots on a spine). The default step cards earn their chrome only when the body adds substance.

antiPatterns.title: Parallel options
antiPatterns.body: If the rows are alternatives the audience compares, use `cards-grid` or `verdict-grid`. The numbered prefix here reads as sequence — using it for parallel items mis-cues the audience.

antiPatterns.title: Author-typed step numbers
antiPatterns.body: Don't write `**STEP 01**` into the markdown. The badge is CSS-generated from the `ol` counter; manual numbering double-stamps and breaks on reordering.

related.name: split-panel
related.when: phase label + heading on the left, steps on the right

related.name: list
related.when: tenets or values (the `principles` variant) rather than a sequence; `takeaway numbered` for gating requirements rather than a sequence of actions

related.name: funnel
related.when: a value-driven funnel with conversion percentages, rather than the qualitative `converge` variant

commonMistakes.mistake: Authoring steps as a bullet list (`-`) instead of a numbered list (`1.`).
commonMistakes.fix: The card chrome — background, border, STEP badge, connector arrow — is scoped to `ol > li` specifically; a `ul` renders as plain unstyled text with no cards, no counter, no badge.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deleting or reordering a step without checking other steps' prose for a stale reference to its old position (e.g. "as covered in step 3").
commonMistakes.fix: The STEP/PHASE/… badge is generated purely from a CSS `counter()` on the `ol` position — it renumbers automatically, but any prose that names a step by number does not.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: The tone is warmer and more editorial than an ops checklist — a personal or reflective process (a practice, a ritual, a habit). One class carries the whole look: centered masthead and cards, a pill badge per step in its own categorical hue, a serif title, no connector arrows, and no masthead hairline. Add `rule-full` if you want the hairline back. Its pill is the card tag at the `inline` placement, centered, in the categorical `--cat-N-mark` tier, so the `tag:` words (`tag-plain`, `tag-none`, `tag-large`, `tag-foot`) restyle it.
The frame is narrow or portrait, or the step bodies need more vertical room — stacks steps down the page instead of across a row.
The story argues through cascading stages (problem → vision → approach → plan) — down-chevron tabs read as a persuasive cascade rather than a neutral sequence.
The process narrows toward one outcome — a qualitative funnel shape without literal conversion percentages (use `funnel` when you have numbers).
The argument is the point and the process is secondary — a faint chevron watermark behind one hero description, editorial in tone.
Steps are light labels with no body copy — dots on a spine, not full description cards.
The audience already thinks of the sequence as phases rather than steps — swaps the badge prefix word; `stage`/`milestone`/`rank`/`tier` swap it to match other vocabularies the same way.
The audience reads order as letters (A, B, C) rather than numbers — swaps the counter format; combine with a prefix-word variant (e.g. `milestone lettered`).
The sequence reads as eras or acts rather than a numbered checklist — swaps the counter format to roman numerals; typically paired with `phase`.

budget.note: hard = the ceiling tools/calibrate-capacity.js --pane measured at 7 words per element, half the slide density (side 65%: clips at 6; stack 50/50: clips at 6). sweet sits below it.

pane.review: side 50 measured, 65 reviewed: step titles break mid-word below 65%.
